objective: Learners compare the total fictional cost of two transportation options, the Crosstown Circuit bus and a QuickHop ride-share estimate, for the same multi-stop trip, and decide which option costs less for that specific plan.
scenario: In the fictional town of Elm Crossing, a Saturday volunteer shift at the Elm Crossing Food Pantry is followed by a stop at the library on the way home. Using the fictional Crosstown Circuit fare table and the fictional QuickHop ride-share estimate printed on this task sheet, the learner models the total cost of each option across all three legs of the trip: home to pantry, pantry to library, and library to home.
materials: the fictional Crosstown Circuit fare table and QuickHop estimate printed on this task sheet

tasks.directions: Compare the two fictional fares for a single ride before looking at the whole trip.

prompts.text: A Crosstown Circuit single ride costs $1.75 and a day pass costs $4.00. A QuickHop ride costs a flat $6.25 no matter the distance within Elm Crossing. If the volunteer only needed one ride today, which option costs less, and by how much?

tasks.directions: Count how many separate ride legs the full trip actually requires before comparing totals.

prompts.text: I counted three separate ride legs: home to pantry, pantry to library, and library to home.
What is the total Crosstown Circuit cost if the volunteer buys three single rides instead of a day pass?

tasks.directions: Model and compare the full trip cost of each option.

prompts.text: Using the fictional fare numbers, calculate the total cost of all three ride legs (home to pantry, pantry to library, library to home) three different ways: three Crosstown Circuit single rides, one Crosstown Circuit day pass, and three separate QuickHop rides. Show each total, then state which single option costs the least for this specific three-leg trip and explain your reasoning in at least two sentences.

tasks.directions: Think about how the comparison would change with a different number of ride legs.

prompts.text: Would the day pass still be the cheapest choice if the volunteer only needed two ride legs instead of three? Explain your reasoning using the fare numbers.

remediation: If a learner treats the day pass as always cheaper regardless of ride count, walk through the break-even point together: divide the day pass price by the single-ride price to find how many rides make the day pass worth it, then apply that number to this trip.
extension: Have the learner add a fourth fictional ride leg to the plan and recalculate all three totals to see whether the cheapest option changes.
